title: Lattice-based NIKE with optimal tightness
authors: Roman Langrehr and Si An Oliver Tran
abstract:
In this work we present a new variant of the non-interactive key exchange (NIKE) scheme based on the learning with errors (LWE) assumption and prove its security with a security reduction that incurs a security loss that is only linear in the number of users. This improves upon all prior reductions for lattice-based NIKE schemes, which had a security loss that is quadratic in the number of users. Our tight reduction can handle the setting with super-polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio and negligible correctness error as well as the more challenging setting with polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio and inverse polynomial correctness error.

We also give a matching lower bound on the tightness for a natural class of  lattice-based NIKE schemes (that captures all existing variants of lattice-based NIKE), showing that our security loss is optimal (up to constant factors). This generalizes a lower bound by Hesse, Hofheinz and Kohl (Crypto 2018) and is the first lower bound for the tightness of lattice-based NIKE schemes. Several previous lower bounds for the tightness of NIKE exist, but none of them can be applied to lattice-based schemes.

                                                         Abstract
           In this work we present a new variant of the non-interactive key exchange (NIKE) scheme based on
       the learning with errors (LWE) assumption and prove its security with a security reduction that incurs
       a security loss that is only linear in the number of users. This improves upon all prior reductions for
       lattice-based NIKE schemes, which had a security loss that is quadratic in the number of users. Our
       tight reduction can handle the setting with super-polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio and negligible
       correctness error as well as the more challenging setting with polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio and
       inverse polynomial correctness error.
           We also give a matching lower bound on the tightness for a natural class of lattice-based NIKE
       schemes (that captures all existing variants of lattice-based NIKE), showing that our security loss is
       optimal (up to constant factors). This generalizes a lower bound by Hesse, Hofheinz and Kohl (Crypto
       2018) and is the first lower bound for the tightness of lattice-based NIKE schemes. Several previous
       lower bounds for the tightness of NIKE exist, but none of them can be applied to lattice-based
       schemes.
           Keywords: Non-interactive key exchange, Learning with errors, Tightness



1      Introduction
Non-interactive key exchange. Non-interactive key exchange (NIKE) is a cryptographic primitive
that allows any pair of users to obtain a common shared key using a public-key infrastructure (PKI) and
no communication (besides what is needed to set up the PKI). More concretely, each user generates a
public/secret key pair and can obtain a shared key with every other user using their own secret key and
the other user’s public key. A famous example of such a scheme is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange [DH76],
which is the basis of many protocols.
   However, with the threat that quantum computers pose on many cryptographic assumptions, such as
the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, it is important to investigate possible post-quantum alternatives. For
NIKE, post-quantum candidates are the isogeny-based schemes CSIDH [Cas+18] and CORAL [Bas+26],
as well as lattice-based constructions.
   The lattice-based NIKE construction appeared in the literature first in works by Ding, Xie, and Lin
[DXL12] and Peikert [Pei14], but the idea of this construction was folklore before these works appeared,
and was subsequently studied in [Guo+20; Lan23; Gaj+24].

Applications. In lattice-based cryptography, it is more common to derive common shared keys by using
a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM), such as the NIST-standardized ML-KEM aka Kyber [Sch+22],
than to use a NIKE. This is because lattice-based KEMs are currently significantly more efficient than
lattice-based NIKEs and much better understood. However, there are several applications of NIKE where
using a KEM instead is difficult or impossible.
    Firstly, changing protocols that are based on NIKEs (such as the Diffie-Hellman key exchange) is a
challenging task that can require significant changes to the protocol and can make additional interaction

or round-trips necessary (see e.g. [SSW20] for TLS, [Hül+21] for WireGuard, and [Ang+22] for the Noise
protocol framework). Secondly, some protocols or schemes rely on the non-interactive nature of NIKE in
way that cannot be replaced by KEMs or other interactive key exchange variants. One such example is
deniable authentication [BMP04; Dod+09; Dam+20; Alw+23; GJK24], which exploits that in a NIKE
scheme both parties can obtain the shared key (at least, assuming that both parties generated their NIKE
key pairs honestly. Without this assumption, deniable authentication seems very challenging to achieve
[FL25]). Another application of NIKE, where a KEM cannot be used instead, is decentralizing functional
encryption [Cho+20; GY24; NPS25].

Security model. The security model we consider in this work is adaptive honest key registration
(HKR) security, introduced in [CKS08; Fre+13]. In this model the adversary can make adaptive queries
to register many users, corrupt these users (which means learning their secret key) and reveal the shared
key between a pair of users. Additionally, the adversary can make a single challenge query where it
obtains a real or random shared key between two users of its choice. The adversary wins if it guesses
correctly which of these two variants was played without making any query that trivially reveals this
challenge shared key.

Tightness. The most widespread approach to analyze the security of a scheme is to give a reduction to
an assumption, that should be much simpler and whose hardness is already well understood. However,
these reductions often come at a loss, meaning that there is a gap between the hardness guarantee of the
scheme compared to the assumption. This is called the security loss and can be, for example, quantified
as follows (as done in [Bad+16, Definiton 9]). The security loss ℓ(r-Λ) of a reduction r-Λ, that runs the
adversary A r times, is a function of the security parameter that satisfies

1.1    Related works on tightness of NIKE
All previous lattice-based NIKE schemes were only proven secure with a security loss of O(N 2 ), where N
is the number of users [DXL12; Pei14; Lan23; Gaj+24]. In fact, most NIKE constructions suffer from this
quadratic security loss. This can be explained with a lower bound by Bader et al. [Bad+16], who show
that a loss of Ω(N 2 ) is unavoidable for a large class of NIKE schemes. Their result captures most NIKE
schemes in the literature, including the traditional Diffie-Hellman key exchange.
    The first work that bypasses their impossibility result is by Hesse, Hofheinz and Kohl [HHK18], who
give a (group-based) NIKE construction that escapes the requirements of their impossibility result and
achieves a O(N ) security loss. They also give a new matching lower bound, that shows that a Ω(N )
security loss is unavoidable for a larger class of NIKEs, including theirs.
    The only NIKE scheme known that can achieve a tighter reduction was presented in [Hes+21] (and
is also group-based). However, this comes at the price of having public and secret keys that grow with
the number of users (which, for concrete efficiency, probably offsets any advantage a tight reduction
might have). If one is willing to allow a key size of O(N ), they get a security loss of only O(log(N )).
They also give a lower bound showing that these large keys are in some sense necessary for such a tight
reduction. This lower bound assumes an inner-product structure of the NIKE. Formally it is incomparable
to the requirements by [Bad+16; HHK18], but it also captures a large number of schemes (including, the
Diffie-Hellman NIKE, the NIKE in [HHK18], and their own scheme). Finally, they combine this with
lattice techniques to reduce the key size at the cost of having a less adaptive security game. For the

purpose of this paper, we do not consider this as a lattice-based scheme because its security can only be
proven based on group and lattice-based assumption (and thus is not a post-quantum scheme).
    Rao [Rao14] gave a lower bound that is similar to [Bad+16] for multi-party NIKE, where a group
of users (and not just pairs of users) can derive a shared key. Their lower bound is exponential in the
maximum size of the group that can derive a common shared key. This lower bound was bypassed only
recently by [KWZ22] with a highly involved construction based on indistinguishability obfuscation.
    Interestingly, none of the previous lower bounds can handle lattice-based NIKE schemes (see Section 2).
One reason is that they all require the NIKE to be perfectly correct, but none of the lattice-based NIKEs
is perfectly correct (and this seems very hard to achieve [Guo+20]). This leaves the problem of what is
the optimal security loss for lattice-based NIKEs wide open.

1.2     Our result
In this work, we present a lattice-based NIKE scheme that has a security loss of O(N ) as well as a
matching lower bound of Ω(N ) that captures a wider class of NIKE schemes than [HHK18], including all
known variants of lattice-based NIKE schemes.
    Technically, we follow the template of [HHK18] to construct a NIKE from a hash-proof system
(HPS). The technical difficulty here is that lattice-based HPSs only achieve weaker properties than their
group-based counterparts that [HHK18] used. This creates some technical challenges, in particular in the
setting with polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio where we have a non-negligible correctness error (which
is in some sense unavoidable [Guo+20]). In this setting, we combine this approach with the techniques
introduced in [Lan23] to prove adaptive HKR security in this setting.
    We then generalize the impossibility result by [HHK18] to capture lattice-based schemes and obtain
our matching lower bound. The difficulty here is that the noise terms that are needed in lattice-based
schemes can cause errors in the resulting shared keys. Even when these errors happen only with negligible
correctness error, they would cause the metareduction argument to fail. We solve these problems by
introducing additional checks on pairs of users, that ensure that all pre-rounding shared keys are far away
from a rounding boundary and thus noise terms cannot cause these errors.
    Similar to previous works, our lower bound captures only reductions that use the adversary in a
black-box way (but can rewind the adversary) and reduce the security to a non-interactive assumption.

1.3     Extensions and open problems
Stronger security models. For many scenarios, a more realistic notion is the variant where the
adversary can make many challenge queries (and either all of them are answered with a real key or all of
them are answered with a random key). This model was previously only considered in [Hes+21]. We
sketch how our positive result (and, in fact, also the one in [HHK18]) can be extended to this setting
without increasing the security loss.
   Another strengthening of the security model is to consider dishonest key registrations (DKR). In this
model, the adversary can register maliciously generated public keys and reveal shared keys of honest users
with these malicious public keys. A generic approach to achieve this security notion is to equip public
keys with a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof of knowledge (NIZKPoK) of the secret key [HHK18].
However, the generic result by [HHK18] requires the NIKE to be perfectly correct and thus cannot be
applied directly to lattice-based schemes. The work [Lan23] showed that this approach can still be used in
combination with the noise smudging technique (which requires super-polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio).
When the NIZKPoK used for this approach is tightly secure, this does not decrease the tightness of the
scheme. Concurrently, [Gaj+24] showed a different approach that uses NIZKPoKs and the (quantum)
random oracle model. Their scheme has a very large security loss that is quadratic in the number of
random oracle queries of the adversary.1
   The technique in [Lan23] is compatible with our NIKE construction with super-polynomial modulus-
to-noise ratio and can be used to upgrade it to DKR security. This upgrade preserves the tightness
assuming the NIZKPoK is tightly secure.

  An interesting open problem is how DKR security can be achieved in the setting with polynomial
modulus-to-noise ratio. The work [Lan23] shows that adding NIZKPoKs is not sufficient in this setting.

Counting corruptions. Moreover, we quantify in this work the security loss by the number of users
the adversary registers. A recent work [Bel+24] argued that it is beneficial to count the number of
corrupted users instead, which is in many real-world scenarios much lower than the number of total users.
They also present a generic framework that shows that in many settings it is possible to get a security
loss that only grows with the number of corrupted users. However, their framework does not capture the
security notions needed for non-interactive key exchange. We leave it as an open problem whether the
security loss for our construction (or NIKEs, in general) can be improved to grow only (linearly) in the
number of corrupted users.
    Such a result would not contradict our lower bound showing that a security loss of Ω(N ) is unavoidable,
because the number of corruptions that the metareduction makes is approximately the same as the total
number of users.

Hash proof systems. From a bird’s eye view, our NIKE has a similar structure to the NIKE in
[HHK18]. This is no coincidence. They give a generic transformation from a hash-proof system to a NIKE
with O(N ) security loss (and a group-based instantiation of this). The core of our NIKE construction
can be seen as instantiating their transformation with a lattice-based hash proof system.
    However, we cannot use their generic transformation as a black-box, since lattice-based hash proof
systems have some limitations that make them unsuitable for their generic result and that require some
lattice-specific tricks to handle. Concretely, the lattice-based hash proof system only provides approximate
correctness. Thus, we present our results in this work without the abstraction of hash proof systems and
elaborate more on the connection to hash proof systems in Appendix C for interested readers.

2.1    Optimality of the tightness.
Finally, we show that our security loss of O(N ) is optimal for lattice-based NIKE (at least, for a natural
structure of lattice-based NIKE schemes that captures all schemes proposed so far). The literature already
has several works that show lower bounds on the tightness of NIKE [Bad+16; HHK18; Hes+21]. However,
none of these results apply to lattice-based NIKE. One reason is that all of these schemes only apply to
perfectly correct NIKE, which none of the existing LWE candidates is (and it seems very challenging to
construct such schemes [Guo+20]). Another reason is that all of them have some requirements on the
NIKE that are not fulfilled by the known lattice-based NIKE constructions.

Metareductions. All the existing lower bounds (as well as the new one we propose) make use of the
metareduction technique, introduced by Coron [Cor02]. For this technique, we assume that the reduction
makes only black-box use of the adversary, (except for rewinding the adversary) and reduces the security
notion, here adaptive HKR security of the NIKE, to any non-interactive assumption.
    Such a reduction is then used to build an adversary B that uses the reduction to attack the underlying
assumption. Therefore, we typically first formulate an inefficient adversary A for the cryptographic scheme
(here, the NIKE), that has a high probability in winning the security game (for example, by brute-force


                                                        6
searching the secret key). Typically, this adversary has probability 1 in winning the game, but in our
case it has a smaller success probability. Depending on the parameters for the LWE-NIKE, it can be for
example overwhelming or a constant less than 1. The adversary B then internally runs the reduction and
tries to efficiently simulate the behavior of A. Assuming that A succeeds, that B successfully simulates
A, and that the reduction is successful, the adversary B breaks the underlying hardness assumption. By
analyzing how successful A and B are and assuming that the underlying assumption is hard, this gives us
a bound on the success probability and therefore tightness of the reduction.
    Next, we briefly revisit each of these metareductions and explain why they cannot capture lattice-based
schemes. For simplicity, we assume for this overview that the reduction does not rewind the adversary.
However, all the results hold even for rewinding reductions.

Quadratic lower bound. The first metareduction for NIKE was published by Bader et al. in [Bad+16].
In their work, the inefficient adversary A first registers N users and performs a check on the public key
for each of them. If all of these checks pass, it selects a random pair of challenge users and asks for the
secret keys for all the other users. Each of these secret keys is then checked if it matches the public key.4
Finally, if all of these checks pass, A brute-force searches a secret key that matches the public key of the
first challenge user, otherwise it outputs ⊥. Of course, honestly generated key pairs should satisfy the
checks performed on the public keys and the public/secret key pairs with high probability, to make sure
that A has high success probability.5 Moreover, these checks need to be efficiently computable, because
they are also executed by B.
    The efficient adversary B now runs the reduction internally and, like A it will also register N users
initially and check the public keys that the reduction outputs. After that, it runs N (N − 1) parallel
copies of the reduction, one for each possible choice of the challenge user pair to retrieve the secret keys
of the remaining users. It then selects one of these runs uniformly at random and tries to successfully
complete only this single one. If the reduction failed to provide a valid secret key for one of the users
in this run, B just outputs ⊥ and then perfectly simulates the behavior of A in this case. Otherwise,
instead of brute-force searching for a secret key for the challenge user, B inspects all the other runs of the
reduction to see if the reduction has returned a valid secret key for one of the challenge users there. If
this is the case, it uses this key to compute the shared key between the challenge users. Otherwise, it
aborts. The probability of aborting can be shown to be in O(1/N 2 ), which implies that the reduction
must have a security loss of Ω(N 2 ).
    To argue that B correctly simulates A when it does not abort, we crucially need the following two
properties
   1. Perfect correctness: We need perfect correctness for all key pairs passing the checks of the
      reduction to argue that the reduction obtains the same shared key for the challenge users, even
      when it only obtained a secret key for the second challenge user (while A always uses the secret
      key for the first challenge user). Even if we allow only a negligible correctness error, this argument

because the reduction actually does not exploit the correctness error of the NIKE (in the sense that

Linear lower bound. Hesse, Hofheinz and Kohl [HHK18] presented a metareduction where there is no
need to check public keys standalone. Instead, they only need a check for public/secret key pairs. They
have a similar requirement for the NIKE as the second requirement above, except that this now only
needs to hold if for both users there is a secret key that matches the public key. This requirement is met
by their group hash proof system based NIKE.
   For the adversary B, it is now important that it obtains the secret key for both challenge users to
ensure that it still simulates A correctly. This happens with probability O(1/N ) and thus they get lower
bound of O(N ) for the security loss of such NIKEs.
   They also mention explicitly perfect correctness as requirement for their metareduction. However,
one can show that the same result holds when dropping the perfect correctness requirement (essentially
because B now anyway needs to get the secret keys for both challenge users).
   However, even when we drop perfect correctness, we cannot apply this result to lattice-based NIKE.
The reason is that the noise terms in the lattice-based NIKE schemes violate also the weaker unique
shared key property that is needed here.

Our new linear lower bound. In this work we show a new metareduction that follows the high-level
strategy of [HHK18], but needs only an even weaker variant of the “unique shared key” property that we
call “pairwise checkable”. We then give a general structure of lattice-based NIKE schemes, that captures
all constructions of this work and previous works for lattice-based NIKEs, and show they satisfy the
requirements of this metareduction.
    Concretely, we replace the validity check for the key pair of a single user with a validity check for each
pair of users. This check gets as input the public-secret key pair of one user (say Alice) and the public
key (but crucially not the secret key!) of another user (say Bob). We now need that when there are two
secret keys for Alice, that both pass this check for Alice’s and Bob’s public key and there is a secret key
for Bob, that passes this check for Bob’s and Alice’s public key, then both of Alice’s secret keys yield the
same shared key for the pair Alice and Bob.
    This property is satisfied by the lattice-based NIKE, because the pairwise check can (apart from doing
validity checks on the individual key pairs) additionally compute the pre-rounding shared key between
Alice and Bob. If this shared key is close to a rounding boundary, the check will fail. If the shared key
is sufficiently far away from the rounding boundaries, the check returns true. This gives us robustness
against small noise terms, because they can influence the pre-rounding shared key only by a small amount.
    In our analysis, we now have to take into account that even honestly generated keys can cause this
check to fail. The result we get here is that the reduction needs to have a security loss of at least
Ω(N (1 − N 2 εPWcheck (λ))), where εPWcheck (λ) is the probability that a pair of honestly generated keys fails
the pairwise check. When we select parameters such that εPWcheck (λ) < 1/(2N 2 ), which is only a mild
requirement on the parameters that can be achieved even with polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio, this
simplifies the lower bound to Ω(N ).

C      The HPS perspective.
NIKE from hash proof systems. Hesse, Hofheinz and Kohl [HHK18] show that we can generically
transform a hash proof system to a NIKE with security loss O(N ). A hash proof system, introduced in
[CS02], is a proof system for an NP relation R where proofs for a statement x (certifying x ∈ L := {x |
∃w : (x, w) ∈ R}) can be generated using a hash public key (sometimes called the projection key) hpk via
a procedure ProjHash(hpk, x, w) that requires both the statement and the witness. Alternatively, one can
generate a proof using the hash secret key hsk via Hash(hsk, x) without the witness w. For correctness,
we require ProjHash(hpk, x, w) = Hash(hsk, x) for all (x, w) ∈ R. The security property we need here is
smoothness, which says that for any x ∈      / L the proof generated via Hash(hsk, x) is uniformly random,
even when given hpk. Moreover, we need that L ⊆ X such that no PPT distinguisher can distinguish a
sample x generated via (x, w) ←   $
                                     R from a uniform sample x ←   $
                                                                     X \ L, except with negligible probability
(subset membership problem).
    This can be turned into an asymmetric NIKE as follows: The left user samples (x, w) ←         $

this as its key pair (i.e., its public key is x and its secret key is w). The right user generates a key pair
(hpk, hsk) and uses this as its key pair for the NIKE (i.e., hpk is its public key and hsk its secret key). The
shared key for two users is simply a proof of the left user’s statement x under the right user’s hashing
keys. The right user, who knows hsk but not w, can compute this proof via Hash and the left user, who
knows w and x but not hsk, can compute this via ProjHash.
    To prove security, the reduction only has to guess the left challenge user and switch its public key to
x← $

problem, the adversary cannot detect this change. With x ∈ X \ L the shared key between the left
challenge user and the right challenge user is uniformly random from the adversary’s point of view. In
fact, the shared keys between the left challenge user and every right user of the system is uniformly
random from the adversary’s point of view.
    In [HHK18], the authors instantiate this with a group-based hash proof system. The difficulty when
instantiating this transformation based on post-quantum assumptions is the lack of suitable hash proof
systems from post-quantum assumptions.
    The first lattice-based hash proof system was introduced in [KV09]. However, their scheme (and all
other lattice-based constructions such as [ZY17; Ben+18]) have the following two limitations:



                                                         41
   1. Approximate correctness: Proofs are elements in Zq and |ProjHash(hpk, x, w) − Hash(hsk, x)|
      is small. To get proofs that are identical with high probability, we can round these values, but
      we cannot get perfect correctness (i.e. guarantee that ProjHash(hpk, x, w) = Hash(hsk, x) always
      holds).

   2. Gap smoothness: The smoothness property only holds for a subset of the statements in X \ L.
      More concretely, in these hash proof systems the language L consists of all vectors close (say, within
      distance B1 ) to a lattice Λ. Smoothness, however, holds only for vectors far away (with distance at
      least B2 ≫ B1 ) from the lattice Λ.
There are some code-based hash proof systems that get rid of the second limitation, but not of the first
limitation [Bet+22; TV23].
    In this work, we observe that the second limitation is unproblematic for the transformation to NIKE.
Namely, as long as there is an (efficiently sampable) distribution such that (1) smoothness holds for
samples of this distribution (with overwhelming probability), and (2) samples from this distribution
are computationally indistinguishable from samples of L. The reason is that in the security proof the
reduction chooses the statements for which smoothness needs to hold. This is in contrast to other
applications of hash proof systems, such as IND-CCA secure public-key encryption, where the adversary
can choose the statement [CS02].
    Secondly, we can also get away with approximate correctness, as long as the correctness error is
negligible. The reason is that then in the security game, with overwhelming probability, in every pair of
users both users obtains the same shared key. This allows the reduction to freely choose which user’s
secret key is used to obtain the shared keys. Of course, the resulting NIKE scheme will then also have a
negligible correctness error.
    Requiring a negligible correctness error is very undesirable for lattice-based scheme, because it requires
a superpolynomial modulus-to-noise ratio, which makes the scheme less efficient. We show that for the
lattice-based instantiation we can even tolerate a non-negligible correctness error when the number of
users is a priori bounded. This result is based on techniques by Langrehr [Lan23] and leverages the
specific structure of lattices (and thus cannot be applied to approximately correct hash proof systems in
general).
